Lessons.Title: Fraction Games
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 5 Unit 3 Lesson 19 'Fraction Games' goal: choose distinct digits from 1,2,3,4,5,6 for the ORIGINAL THREE printed expression types, and build both largest and smallest possible positive product or quotient. The actual mathematical source task includes a/b × c/d, n ÷ (1/d), and (1/d) ÷ n; each expression uses each chosen number no more than once. Do not claim a fixed choice-only oracle assesses the learner's optimization proof.

Warm-up original Estimation Exploration: 28 × 2 8/9. Because 2 8/9 is slightly below 3, product is just below 28×3=84 and above 28×2=56. Exact result 28×26/9=728/9=80 8/9. Student low/about-right/high estimate reasoning is teacher reviewed.

Activity 1 LARGEST: for fraction product four distinct slots, if improper fractions are permitted as in the source unqualified a/b form, (6/1)×(5/2)=15 is optimal using the largest two numerators and smallest two denominators. Whole ÷ unit fraction: 6÷(1/5)=30 or 5÷(1/6)=30. Unit fraction ÷ whole: (1/2)÷1=1/2 with distinct digits 2 and 1. Students explain all legal assignments, including swapped factor ties; teacher reviews their argument about whether any additional source classroom restrictions are imposed.

Activity 2 SMALLEST: fraction product (1/6)×(2/5)=1/15 with four distinct digit slots. Whole ÷ unit fraction: 1÷(1/2)=2. Unit fraction ÷ whole: (1/6)÷5=1/30, or (1/5)÷6=1/30. Mathematical constraints and source permitted digits are essential; choosing a digit twice violates the original problem even when the arithmetic is correct.

Assessment: source asks student pairs to justify largest AND smallest in all three expression shapes, not only one division question. A selected exact numeric answer is supplemental; legality, optimality proof, source digits, partner discussion and alternative tied solutions are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Original source Cool-down gated and figure binaries not claimed verified. Independent Edulytiks teacher Cool-down checks a new exact optimization scenario.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division by a unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Division asks how many unit-fraction groups fit in an amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For positive integers a,b, a ÷ (1/b) = a × b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction divided by a whole number
KeyConcepts.Definition: The unit fraction is split into equal smaller parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Maximum and minimum under constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: An extreme value must respect every allowed digit and use restriction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: To maximize a×b with distinct digits 1–6 choose 6 and 5; to minimize 1/(ab), maximize the same positive denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Justifying the best choice
KeyConcepts.Definition: A good candidate is not enough without reasoning that no permitted alternative is better.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare factors and show that replacing one selected digit by an unused larger digit increases a positive product.
KeyConcepts.Example: A legal pair (4,6) makes 24, less than (5,6) making 30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate and compute 28×2 8/9.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare mixed number against 2 and 3 then exact fraction conversion.
Steps: Convert 728/9 to 80 8/9 and explain why close to 84.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source three largest expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Fill the three source templates using distinct digits 1–6 for each expression to give a greatest value.
WorkedExamples.Method: Product/quotient monotonicity by digit position, teacher reviews proof.
Steps: a/b×c/d: use 6,5 on top and 1,2 below ->15.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 15, 30, 1/2 respectively, under source's unrestricted positive-digit slots.
WorkedExamples.Check: No chosen digit repeats in an expression; equivalent source-permitted ties possible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source three smallest expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Fill each original source template with legal distinct digits to minimize its positive value.
WorkedExamples.Method: Put smallest numerators/largest denominators; compare division forms.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks global optimality explanation, not just chosen numeric outcome.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Largest whole ÷ unit fraction
WorkedExamples.Question: With distinct digits 1–6 in a ÷ (1/b), what is the greatest possible quotient?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the inverse relation a ÷ (1/b) = a × b, then optimize the product.
Steps: All candidates are products of two distinct positive digits up to six.
The two largest different digits are six and five.
Compute 6 ÷ (1/5) = 6 × 5 = 30 and give a reason smaller digits cannot exceed this.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both use distinct legal digits; any other pair has at least one factor smaller than 5 or 6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Smallest unit fraction ÷ whole
WorkedExamples.Question: With distinct digits 1–6 in (1/a) ÷ b, what is the least positive quotient?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert the quotient to the reciprocal of a product and maximize its denominator.
Steps: The largest product of two distinct allowed digits is 6×5 = 30.
WorkedExamples.Check: For positive denominators, 1/30 is smaller than 1/k for every positive k under 30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Estimate a fractional product
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 28 × 2 8/9, then calculate exactly.
WorkedExamples.Method: Bound the mixed number between two whole numbers before multiplying.
Steps: The mixed number is close to 3, so expect a product a little smaller than 84.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 80 8/9; an estimate of roughly 81 is sensible.
WorkedExamples.Check: 80 8/9 is between 56 and 84 and close to 84, as expected.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Division always makes the number smaller
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction such as 1/5 counts many small groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 6 ÷ (1/5) = 30 to check which interpretation the question uses.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A large-looking fraction automatically makes the best expression
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing a numerator or denominator has a different effect depending on whether the fraction is the divisor or dividend.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rewrite the exact expression as a product or reciprocal, then compare legal digit assignments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A correct extreme value is a complete argument
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Finding 30 or 1/30 does not, by itself, establish that no other permitted choice is better.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain why the two largest distinct legal digits give the greatest positive product.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Score only one source fraction division optimum and omit fraction-by-fraction product and the opposite extreme
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original 2021 activities ask six global extrema over three different expression types, with digit uniqueness, requiring strategy and proof.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Cover all three source templates twice (maximum and minimum), check distinct digits and teacher-reviewed optimality argument.

SummaryPoints: Source asks BOTH maximum and minimum for all THREE printed fraction product/quotient templates.
Use distinct chosen digits 1–6 per expression; repeated digits invalidate an otherwise right calculation.
Math extrema under unrestricted source templates: products 15 and 1/15; whole÷fraction 30 and 2; fraction÷whole 1/2 and 1/30.
Teacher checks global maximal/minimal reasoning, legal source number reuse constraints and partner exchange; numeric digital cases insufficient alone.
